note: Each module takes about 3 minutes: a short intro, one hands-on activity and a 3-question quiz. Passing (2 of 3 or better) unlocks a certificate with the staff member's name. All examples are invented.

modules.title: Spot the fake invoice
modules.intro: Invoice fraud is when a criminal sends an invoice, or a 'bank details have changed' note, so that a real payment goes to their account instead. It works because it looks like normal paperwork.

activity.prompt: Tap the four things on this invoice email that should make you stop and check.

lines.text: Hello, please find invoice KP-0931 attached for £2,365.40.
Our bank has changed, so please pay to the new account below.
This invoice is now overdue. Please pay today to avoid a late fee.
Please reply to this email to confirm once paid, rather than calling, as our phones are down.

hotspots.h1: The address is 'kestrelprint-co.uk', not the 'kestrelprint.co.uk' you've used before. One extra hyphen.
hotspots.h2: A change of bank details. Always phone on a number you already have before paying.
hotspots.h3: Pressure to pay today. Real suppliers can wait for you to check.
hotspots.h4: Trying to stop you phoning. That's exactly the check that would catch it.

quiz.q: A regular supplier emails to say their bank details have changed. What should you do first?
options: Update the details and pay as normal
Reply to the email to confirm
Phone the supplier on a number you already have
Wait for a second email
quiz.explain: Phoning on a number you already have is the one check that reliably catches invoice fraud. Replying goes straight back to the scammer.

quiz.q: Which of these is a sign of a lookalike email address?
options: The email has your supplier's logo
The address is accounts@harbourmi11foods.co.uk instead of harbourmillfoods.co.uk
The email arrived on a Monday
The invoice number is new
quiz.explain: Swapping a letter for a number is a common trick. Logos are easy to copy, so they prove nothing.

quiz.q: Why do scammers often say an invoice is overdue?
options: To be polite
To rush you so you don't check
Because it's a legal requirement
To get a discount
quiz.explain: Urgency is designed to stop you thinking or checking with anyone.

modules.title: Spot the phishing email
modules.intro: Phishing is a fake message designed to make you click a link, enter a password or open a harmful file. AI now writes these without spelling mistakes, so judge an email by what it asks you to do, not how well it's written.

activity.prompt: Tap the four warning signs in this email.

item.subject: We tried to deliver your parcel

lines.text: We were unable to deliver your parcel today because of an unpaid fee of £1.99.
Pay within 24 hours or your parcel will be returned to the sender.
You will need to enter your card details and email password to confirm your identity.

hotspots.h1: A generic greeting. Companies you deal with usually use your name.
hotspots.h2: A deadline and a threat, to rush you.
hotspots.h3: A link to a website you don't recognise. Go to the courier's site yourself instead.
hotspots.h4: No delivery company needs your email password. This is the real goal.

quiz.q: An email is perfectly written, with no spelling mistakes. Does that mean it's genuine?
options: Yes, scam emails always have mistakes
No, AI now writes scam emails without mistakes
Only if it has a logo
Only if it's from a big company
quiz.explain: The NCSC says AI helps criminals write convincing phishing without the mistakes that used to give it away.

quiz.q: You clicked a link in an email and then realised it was fake. What should you do?
options: Say nothing and hope for the best
Tell the person who handles IT straight away
Delete the email and carry on
Forward it to everyone as a warning
quiz.explain: The sooner someone knows, the less damage it does. You won't be in trouble for reporting it.

quiz.q: Where can you forward a suspicious email in the UK?
options: report@phishing.gov.uk
The sender, to ask if it's real
Your bank's general email
Nowhere, just delete it
quiz.explain: The NCSC's free reporting service checks the email and can take down the scam website.

modules.title: Safe and unsafe AI prompts
modules.intro: AI tools can save time, but whatever you type in has left the business. The simple rule: describe the situation, not the person. Never paste customer details, staff records, passwords or bank details.

activity.prompt: Sort each prompt into 'Fine' or 'Never put this into an AI tool'.

bins.label: Never put this into an AI tool

items.text: Write a friendly reply to a customer whose order arrived late, offering a 10% discount.
items.why: No personal details, just the situation.

items.text: Here's Sarah Jones's complaint email with her address and order history. Write a reply.
items.why: It contains a named customer's personal details. Describe the situation instead.

items.text: Suggest five Instagram captions for our new spring menu.
items.why: Public marketing content with nothing confidential.

items.text: Here is our staff spreadsheet with salaries and home addresses. Make it into a nice table.
items.why: Staff personal and pay details should never go into an AI tool.

items.text: Check the grammar of this paragraph from our website's About page.
Our bank login keeps failing. Here's the username and password, what's wrong?
items.why: Never share passwords with anyone, including AI tools.

items.text: Explain in plain English what 'data minimisation' means for a small salon.
items.why: A general question with no personal or confidential data.

items.text: Summarise this client's medical history so I can prepare for their appointment.
items.why: Health information is especially sensitive personal data.

items.text: Draft a polite payment reminder for an invoice that's 14 days overdue.
items.why: A template with no names or account details.

items.text: Here's our supplier contract, which is marked confidential. Find any risks.
items.why: Confidential business documents shouldn't leave the business without approval.

quiz.q: What's the simplest rule for using AI tools safely at work?
options: Only use AI on Fridays
Describe the situation, not the person
Always paste the full email for context
Use any free tool you like
quiz.explain: Leaving out names and identifying details usually gives just as good an answer, and keeps personal data in the business.

quiz.q: An AI tool writes a reply promising a customer a full refund. What should you do?
options: Send it, the AI knows best
Check it against your refund policy before sending
Ask the AI if it's sure
Send it and correct it later if needed
quiz.explain: AI can state wrong things confidently. A person checks anything before it reaches a customer.

quiz.q: Which of these should never go into an AI tool?
options: A question about grammar
Ideas for a social media post
A customer's name, address and order history
A general question about the law
quiz.explain: Customer details are personal data and shouldn't be pasted into AI tools.

modules.title: The urgent call from the boss
modules.intro: Criminals now use AI to copy a person's voice or face from a few online clips. They pretend to be the boss or a supplier and ask for an urgent payment. The fix is simple: hang up and call back on a number you already have.

activity.prompt: Choose what you'd do at each step.

steps.situation: At 4.40pm your phone rings from an unknown number. It sounds exactly like the owner: 'My phone's died, I'm on a borrowed one. I need you to pay a new supplier £3,200 before the bank closes.'

choices.text: Make the payment, it's definitely their voice
choices.feedback: A voice can be copied with AI. Recognising it isn't proof.

choices.text: Say you'll call them straight back, then hang up
choices.feedback: Right. Ending the call puts you back in control.

choices.text: Ask them a few questions to check it's really them
choices.feedback: Better than paying, but a scammer may know the answers from social media. Calling back is stronger.

steps.situation: You hang up. Which number do you call?

choices.text: The number they just called from
choices.feedback: That goes straight back to the caller.

choices.text: The owner's usual number saved in your phone
choices.feedback: Yes. Only a number you already have reaches the real person.

choices.text: A number they texted you afterwards
choices.feedback: Any number sent by the caller could be theirs.

steps.situation: The owner doesn't answer their usual number. The 'supplier' emails asking why the money hasn't arrived.

choices.feedback: Pressure from the 'supplier' is another warning sign.

choices.text: Wait, and keep trying the owner or another senior person you trust
choices.feedback: Correct. A genuine payment can wait. A scam can't.

choices.text: Pay half to keep them happy
choices.feedback: Any payment to an unchecked account is at risk.

quiz.q: Can criminals copy someone's voice with AI?
options: No, voices can't be faked
Yes, from short clips found online
Only famous people's voices
Only on video calls
quiz.explain: Government fraud guidance warns that criminals use deepfake audio or video to impersonate senior people.

quiz.q: The 'boss' asks for an urgent payment by voice note from a new number. What do you do?
options: Pay quickly so they're not kept waiting
Reply to the voice note asking if it's real
Call the boss back on the number you already have
Forward it to a colleague to pay
quiz.explain: Call back on a known number. Never use contact details from the message itself.

quiz.q: If money has already been sent to a scammer, who should you call first?
options: Your bank, straight away
The scammer, to ask for it back
Nobody, it's too late
Your accountant at the end of the month
quiz.explain: Calling your bank quickly gives the best chance of stopping the payment. Then report it to Report Fraud on 0300 123 2040.
